title: Basu's theorem

title: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Brouwer's fixed-point theorem is a fixed-point theorem in topology, named after L. E. J. Brouwer. The simplest forms of Brouwer's theorem are for continuous functions $f$ from a closed interval $I$ in the real numbers to itself or from a closed disk $D$ to itself. A more general form than the latter is for continuous functions from a nonempty convex compact subset $K$ of Euclidean space to itself.

title: Carathéodory's theorem (convex hull)
source_statement_excerpt: Carathéodory's theorem is a theorem in convex geometry. It states that if a point $x$ lies in the convex hull $\mathrm {Conv} (P)$ of a set $P\subset \mathbb {R} ^{d}$ , then $x$ lies in some $d$ -dimensional simplex with vertices in $P$ . Equivalently, $x$ can be written as the convex combination of $d+1$ or fewer points in $P$ . Additionally, $x$ can be written as the convex combination of at most $d+1$ extremal points in $P$ , as non-extremal points can be removed from $P$ without changing the membership of $x$ in the convex hull.
statement: Assume $P\subseteq\mathbb R^d$; $x\in\operatorname{conv}(P)$. There are at most $d+1$ points $p_1,\dots,p_k\in P$ and nonnegative coefficients $\lambda_i$ summing to 1 such that $x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i p_i$.
conclusions: There are at most $d+1$ points $p_1,\dots,p_k\in P$ and nonnegative coefficients $\lambda_i$ summing to 1 such that $x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i p_i$.

title: Cross's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle in the Euclidean plane. Suppose squares $DABE$ , $FBCG$ , and $HCAI$ are drawn on the outside of $\triangle ABC$ . Then the areas of the four triangles $\triangle ABC$ , $\triangle AID$ , $\triangle BEF$ , and $\triangle CGH$ are equal.
statement: Assume $ABC$ is a Euclidean triangle; Squares $DABE$, $FBCG$, and $HCAI$ are constructed externally on its sides. The triangles $ABC$, $AID$, $BEF$, and $CGH$ all have equal area.
hypotheses: Squares $DABE$, $FBCG$, and $HCAI$ are constructed externally on its sides
conclusions: The triangles $ABC$, $AID$, $BEF$, and $CGH$ all have equal area.

title: Darboux's theorem (analysis)
source_statement_excerpt: Let $I$ be an open interval, and let $f\colon I\to \mathbb {R} $ be a real-valued differentiable function. Then $f'$ has the intermediate value property: If $a$ and $b$ are points in $I$ with $a<b$ , then for every $y$ between $f'(a)$ and $f'(b)$ , there exists an $x$ in $[a,b]$ such that $f'(x)=y$ .
statement: Assume $I$ is an open interval; $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable; $a,b\in I$ with $a<b$; $y$ lies between $f'(a)$ and $f'(b)$. There exists $x\in[a,b]$ with $f'(x)=y$.
conclusions: There exists $x\in[a,b]$ with $f'(x)=y$.
editorial_note: Explicit intermediate-value formulation for the derivative.

$t$ denotes the number of distinct lines determined by pairs of points of $P$

title: Dejean's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $k$ be the number of symbols in an alphabet. For every $k$ , define $\operatorname {RT} (k)$ , the repeat threshold, to be the infimum of exponents $e$ such that there exists an infinite $e$ -power-free word on a $k$ -symbol alphabet. Thus, for instance, the Thue–Morse sequence shows that $\operatorname {RT} (2)=2$ , and an argument based on the Lovász local lemma can be used to show that $\operatorname {RT} (k)$ is finite for all $k$ .

title: Dini's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: If $X$ is a compact topological space, and $(f_{n})_{n\in \mathbb {N} }$ is a monotonically increasing sequence (meaning $f_{n}(x)\leq f_{n+1}(x)$ for all $n\in \mathbb {N} $ and $x\in X$ ) of continuous real-valued functions on $X$ which converges pointwise to a continuous function $f\colon X\to \mathbb {R} $ , then the convergence is uniform. The same conclusion holds if $(f_{n})_{n\in \mathbb {N} }$ is monotonically decreasing instead of increasing.
statement: Assume $X$ is a compact topological space; $(f_n)$ is a pointwise monotone sequence of continuous real-valued functions on $X$; $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ for every $x\in X$; $f$ is continuous. $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $X$.
hypotheses: $(f_n)$ is a pointwise monotone sequence of continuous real-valued functions on $X$
conclusions: $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $X$.
editorial_note: Both monotone increasing and monotone decreasing cases included.

title: Discontinuities of monotone functions
source_statement_excerpt: If $f\left(x^{+}\right)$ and $f\left(x^{-}\right)$ exist and are finite then the difference $f\left(x^{+}\right)-f\left(x^{-}\right)$ is called the jump of $f$ at $x.$
statement: Assume $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is monotone on an interval $I$. Every interior discontinuity of $f$ is a jump discontinuity, and the set of discontinuities is at most countable.
hypotheses: $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is monotone on an interval $I$
conclusions: Every interior discontinuity of $f$ is a jump discontinuity, and the set of discontinuities is at most countable.
editorial_note: Used main theorem in lead, not selected definition of jump.

title: Dominated convergence theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In measure theory, Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem gives a mild sufficient condition under which limits and integrals of a sequence of functions can be interchanged. More technically it says that if a sequence of functions is bounded in absolute value by an integrable function and is almost everywhere pointwise convergent to a function then the sequence converges in $L_{1}$ to its pointwise limit, and in particular the integral of the limit is the limit of the integrals. Its power and utility are two of the primary theoretical advantages of Lebesgue integration over Riemann integration.
statement: Assume $(S,\Sigma,\mu)$ is a measure space; $f_n$ are measurable complex-valued functions converging almost everywhere to $f$; There exists $g\in L^1(\mu)$ with $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for all $n$. $f,f_n\in L^1(\mu)$, $\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\to0$, and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$.
hypotheses: $f_n$ are measurable complex-valued functions converging almost everywhere to $f$
There exists $g\in L^1(\mu)$ with $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for all $n$
conclusions: $f,f_n\in L^1(\mu)$, $\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\to0$, and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$.
editorial_note: Included stronger L1 conclusion given in the Statement section.

title: Doob decomposition theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $(\Omega ,{\mathcal {F}},\mathbb {P} )$ be a probability space, I = {0, 1, 2, ..., N} with $N\in \mathbb {N} $ or $I=\mathbb {N} _{0}$ a finite or countably infinite index set, $({\mathcal {F}}_{n})_{n\in I}$ a filtration of ${\mathcal {F}}$ , and X = (Xn)n∈I an adapted stochastic process with E[|Xn|] < ∞ for all n ∈ I. Then there exist a martingale M = (Mn)n∈I and an integrable predictable process A = (An)n∈I starting with A0 = 0 such that Xn = Mn + An for every n ∈ I. Here predictable means that An is ${\mathcal {F}}_{n-1}$ -measurable for every n ∈ I \ {0}. This decomposition is almost surely unique.
statement: Assume $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a discrete-time filtration over an index set $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ or $\mathbb N_0$; $(X_n)$ is adapted with $\mathbb E|X_n|<\infty$ for all $n$. There exist a martingale $(M_n)$ and an integrable predictable process $(A_n)$ with $A_0=0$ and $X_n=M_n+A_n$ for all $n$, and the decomposition is unique up to almost-sure equality.
hypotheses: $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a discrete-time filtration over an index set $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ or $\mathbb N_0$
$(X_n)$ is adapted with $\mathbb E|X_n|<\infty$ for all $n$
conclusions: There exist a martingale $(M_n)$ and an integrable predictable process $(A_n)$ with $A_0=0$ and $X_n=M_n+A_n$ for all $n$, and the decomposition is unique up to almost-sure equality.

title: Dugundji extension theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $X$ be a metrizable space, $A$ a closed subset of X, and $L$ a locally convex topological vector space. Then: Every continuous map $f:A\to L$ admits a continuous extension $F:X\to L$ such that the image $F(X)$ is contained in the convex hull of $f(A).$
statement: Assume $X$ is metrizable; $A\subseteq X$ is closed; $L$ is a locally convex topological vector space; $f:A\to L$ is continuous. There exists a continuous extension $F:X\to L$ of $f$ with $F(X)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(f(A))$.
hypotheses: $L$ is a locally convex topological vector space
conclusions: There exists a continuous extension $F:X\to L$ of $f$ with $F(X)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(f(A))$.
editorial_note: Kept the stronger convex-hull conclusion from the formal statement.

title: Earle–Hamilton fixed-point theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, the Earle–Hamilton fixed point theorem is a result in geometric function theory giving sufficient conditions for a holomorphic mapping of an open domain in a complex Banach space into itself to have a fixed point. The result was proved in 1968 by Clifford Earle and Richard S. Hamilton by showing that, with respect to the Carathéodory metric on the domain, the holomorphic mapping becomes a contraction mapping to which the Banach fixed-point theorem can be applied.
statement: Assume $D$ is a connected open subset of a complex Banach space; $f:D\to D$ is holomorphic; $f(D)$ is norm bounded; $f(D)$ has positive distance from the complement of $D$. $f$ has a unique fixed point $x\in D$ and $f^{\circ n}(y)\to x$ for every $y\in D$.
hypotheses: $D$ is a connected open subset of a complex Banach space
$f(D)$ has positive distance from the complement of $D$
conclusions: $f$ has a unique fixed point $x\in D$ and $f^{\circ n}(y)\to x$ for every $y\in D$.
editorial_note: Central theorem separated directly from source statement.

title: Eilenberg's inequality
